title: Dry May-June weather was followed by more spongy moth defoliation in the next year in eastern US aerial surveys, 1999-2025; forest tent caterpillar did not show this
abstract: Question: do dry early summers come before growth of spongy moth (Lymantria dispar dispar) defoliation? The fungus Entomophaga maimaiga needs rain in May-June to kill the larvae, and agencies said that dry springs caused the 2015-2018 and 2020-2022 outbreaks. Approach: we rasterized USFS Insect and Disease Survey defoliation and surveyed-area polygons (Regions 8 and 9, 1997-2025) into 0.25-degree cells and used NOAA nClimGrid rain. A pre-registered fixed-effects model related log growth of defoliated area from year t to t+1 to May-June rain in year t, with density, rain in t+1 and survey-coverage rules. Results: in 1,066 cells and 15,042 transitions, May-June rain 1 SD above normal (about 28% more rain) gave -0.173 (95% CI -0.235 to -0.112) lower growth. No permutation of whole-year rain maps among years gave a coefficient this far from zero (p = 0.0005). The coefficient was negative in New England (-0.18), the Mid-Atlantic (-0.30) and the Great Lakes (-0.06, not clear), in 1999-2011 and 2012-2024, in both survey eras and with year fixed effects. Forest tent caterpillar, which the fungus does not infect, gave -0.002. Rain in March-April, July, August-September and two years later gave near-zero values. Where defoliation was present, 1 SD drier weather gave about 1.6 times more next-year area. Limitations: aerial sketch maps are approximate and survey coverage changed (very low in 2020); we did not measure infection, so the mechanism is not proven; rain improved forward forecasts of 2015-2024 cell growth by only 1.9%; the 2020-2021 increase did not follow a dry May-June in covered cells. Code, plan, derived cell-year panel and figures are included; raw files stay at the public sources.

citations.reason: Earlier campaign IDS study of western bark beetles with the same rasterization approach; it pooled defoliators and did not test a defoliator-specific weather link, which this work does.
Review of E. maimaiga epizootiology; moisture dependence of infection is the tested mechanism.
